articles.title: A New York woman says co-op staff entered her apartment while she was out, took her dog and cat, and concealed where the dog went; three years later, an appeals court has let her trespass and distress claims proceed
articles.summary: A New York woman who accused employees of her housing cooperative of entering her apartment without permission and taking away her dog and cat has won a
articles.body: A New York woman who accused employees of her housing cooperative of entering her apartment without permission and taking away her dog and cat has won a legal battle to continue pursuing two of her claims. Nearly three years after the incident, a New York appeals court ruled on Wednesday, that Lisa Cinque could proceed with her claims of trespass and intentional infliction of emotional distress against Glen Oaks Village Owners, Inc, and its employees.Cinque alleged that the employees entered her apartment while she was away, removed her pets and later gave her misleading information about where her dog had been taken. She said she repeatedly tried to locate the animal but was unsuccessful. According to Justia, documents submitted during the case indicated that the dog had spent nearly two months at a shelter before being euthanised.On May 31, when Cinque, a shareholder in the cooperative housing corporation and a resident of one of its apartments, was away from home, two employees, Gina Catania and Justin Conklin, allegedly forced their way into the apartment without her consent. According to her, they searched through her belongings, took photographs, removed personal property, including her dog and cat, and left the apartment door open.The employees then gave her cat to a neighbour. Finding her dog, however, became a prolonged struggle. Cinque claimed that the defendants initially refused to tell her where the animal had been taken. When they eventually provided information, she said it led her to facilities that could not locate her pet.Dog gets euthanisedAccording to the court judgment, the defendants first told Cinque that her dog had been taken to "Animal Care and Control". She contacted several facilities but could not find it.Her lawyer subsequently demanded information about the animal's location. In response, the defendants said the dog had been taken to the Humane Society of New York. Cinque contacted that organisation as well, but it denied receiving her dog.She continued seeking answers, but the complaint alleged that the defendants refused to provide further information. Cinque accused them of deliberately making false statements that prevented her from discovering where her pet was being kept.The court records also revealed what the defendants submitted in their attempt to have the lawsuit dismissed. They produced veterinary records covering May to July 2023, which they said concerned Cinque's dog.Those records indicated that a dog had arrived at a shelter on May 31, 2023, and had been described to shelter employees as an abandoned animal without an owner. After remaining there for almost two months, the dog was euthanised on July 24, 2023.'Apartment entry was emergency'Cinque filed her lawsuit in September 2023, seeking damages for trespass, intentional infliction of emotional distress and prima facie tort.The defendants disputed the basis of her claims and asked the court to dismiss the complaint before filing an answer.They argued that a foul odour coming from Cinque's apartment had created an emergency that justified their entry. To support their position, they submitted the apartment's proprietary lease, the cooperative's house rules and what they described as body-camera footage of the incident.The lease and house rules allowed employees to enter an apartment in an emergency. The defendants maintained that the smell coming from Cinque's home met that condition.However, Cinque argued that the material submitted by the defendants did not conclusively disprove her allegations.On February 25, 2025, a court in Queens County refused to dismiss any of her claims. The defendants then appealed that decision, bringing the dispute before the Appellate Division, Second Department.Appeals court allows two claims to continueIn its November 4 ruling, the appeals court examined whether Cinque's allegations were sufficient for the lawsuit to proceed.On the trespass claim, the judges found that Cinque had alleged an unauthorised and forceful entry into her apartment. They also concluded that the defendants' evidence did not conclusively establish that the entry was legally justified. The court therefore allowed the trespass claim to continue.The judges reached a similar conclusion regarding the emotional distress claim. They considered Cinque's allegations that her pets had been removed, that information about her dog had repeatedly been withheld or misrepresented, and that the animal had eventually been euthanised after being taken to a shelter.The court found that these allegations were sufficient to support a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress at this stage of the proceedings.However, the judges dismissed Cinque's third claim, known as prima facie tort. They found that her complaint did not adequately establish the required allegations concerning the defendants' motivation or identify specific financial losses.The appeals court consequently modified the lower court's order, dismissing only the prima facie tort claim while allowing the other two claims to proceed. It also awarded costs to Cinque.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Immigration after the midterms: A new Congress, but who holds the power?
articles.summary: Democrats’ takeover of the House and Senate promises greater scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.
articles.body: Democrats’ takeover of the House and Senate promises greater scrutiny of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda. But with the President’s executive powers intact and several major policy battles already before the courts, H-1B workers, Indian students and H-4 spouses may have to wait for relief.The Democratic Party’s victories in the US midterm elections have changed the balance of power in Washington, with the party securing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. But for millions of immigrants, international students and foreign professionals, particularly those on H-1B visas, the more important question is whether the change in Congress will translate into a change in immigration policy.The answer, according to immigration attorneys and policy experts, is far from straightforward.Democrats have secured at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate and, in the preliminary House tally, at least 231 seats against 141 for Republicans, with several races still being counted. The results give Democrats control of both chambers for the first time during President Donald Trump’s current term. The new Congress, the 120th, takes office on Jan 3, 2027.The change gives Democrats considerable powers of oversight and the ability to scrutinise the administration’s immigration policies. But it does not give them the power to automatically reverse executive orders, presidential proclamations or regulations already issued by federal agencies. That distinction is central to understanding what the election could mean for legal immigration.Cyrus Mehta, an immigration attorney, cautions against expecting an immediate change in direction. Notwithstanding the midterm results, he says, the President retains the authority to issue regulations and policies through executive action.“While there may be oversight committee investigations into ICE excesses and abuses, and DHS racial profiling, I think the administration will pretty much carry out its immigration agenda,” Mehta says.He believes the administration will continue to rely on executive powers, regulations and policy memoranda, particularly because passing major legislation in the Senate generally requires overcoming the 60-vote threshold.“Congress may be able to question the administration regarding the justification for the $100,000 H-1B fee for hiring workers from outside the US, but its authority is limited to just that: holding hearings and asking questions. The administration will continue to implement rules and policies,” he adds.Ashwin Sharma, a Jacksonville-based attorney, points out that a presidential proclamation can be revoked by the President who issued it or struck down by a court. A final regulation can be undone through new rulemaking or a Congressional Review Act resolution, although the President could veto such a resolution.Sharma adds, “What the new majorities actually hold is the power to deny appropriations to specific rules, the power to investigate and subpoena, and, in the Senate, the power to decline nominees and judges. Those are real, and they should take the most reckless anti-immigration tactics off the table. But they do not reverse the immigration agenda. Washington changed who holds the gavel, but not who holds the pen: for the next two years, immigration policy will be drafted in the West Wing and redlined in the federal courts.”Rajiv S. Khanna, managing attorney at Immigration.com, offers a more detailed account of the tools available to the incoming Democratic majority. Congress, he says, can narrow the authority delegated to the executive through legislation, prohibit particular fees or write programmes such as OPT and H-4 employment authorisation into statute.But there is a significant obstacle: the presidential veto. A bill must be signed by the President to become law, unless Congress secures a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a veto.Khanna believes Democrats could instead use spending legislation to attach restrictions on funding for particular immigration policies. They can also use congressional oversight to demand documents and testimony from officials responsible for implementing controversial measures.The Congressional Review Act offers another possible route for challenging certain final agency regulations. It allows Congress to pass resolutions of disapproval through an expedited process, although such a resolution still faces the possibility of a presidential veto. Proposed regulations and presidential proclamations are not covered in the same way.Duden Freeman, a former senior official with the US Department of State (DOS), similarly cautions that a change in congressional control should not be confused with comprehensive immigration reform. “While the shift in Congress indicates increased accountability and oversight of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and DOS, I don’t expect most visa policies to change drastically,” she says.“Everything the administration does that is not in line with the Constitution is taken to the relevant courts anyway,” Freeman says. She adds that real immigration reform may be easier to pass with a Democratic Congress but harder to secure with Trump in the White House.For Doug Rand, a former senior official with DHS, the courts may prove to be the more consequential check on the administration’s immigration policies.“The most important check on Trump’s immigration actions may not be the new Congress, but rather the courts. The original $100K H-1B fee was already blocked by a federal judge, and similar attempts to restrict legal immigration will likely meet the same fate,” Rand says.The question, therefore, is not simply what Democrats can undo after January 3, but which of the administration’s policies can survive legal scrutiny.H-1B: One fee blocked, another proposedThe H-1B programme is likely to remain among the most closely watched areas of immigration policy, particularly for Indian technology professionals and the employers who sponsor them.The Trump administration’s $100K payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions has encountered substantial legal resistance. A federal court in Massachusetts vacated the policy implementing the payment in June 2026, and the First Circuit declined to suspend that ruling in July. A second federal court in California blocked the fee in Sept. The administration has extended the underlying presidential proclamation through Sept 2027, but the fee remains blocked under the relevant court orders.However, a separate proposal could create another financial hurdle. DHS has proposed a $103K fee for certain cap-subject H-1B petitions through formal rulemaking. As of the date of this draft, it remains a proposal rather than an implemented fee.Kripa Upadhyay, an immigration attorney and partner at Buchalter, says: “While Congress could increase scrutiny and try to restrict the administration’s ability to collect the proposed H-1B fee by attaching a condition to government funding legislation, it cannot simply stop the separate regulatory process.”Snehal Batra, managing attorney at NPZ&B, makes a similar point, noting that the administration is pursuing many of its immigration priorities through executive action and agency rulemaking rather than legislation.“The President retains significant authority over immigration and can direct agencies like DHS, USCIS and ICE to pursue enforcement and regulatory priorities. While Democrats can increase oversight through hearings and investigations and make it more difficult to pass new restrictive legislation, they cannot simply undo existing executive actions. As a result, I expect the administration to continue advancing its immigration agenda through the executive branch, with many of the key battles playing out in the courts through challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act rather than in Congress,” she explains.Proposed increase in prevailing wages for H-1B and PERM positionsAnother concern is the proposed increase in prevailing wages for H-1B and employment-based green card programmes.Currently, wages are pegged to four levels at roughly the 17th, 34th, 50th and 67th percentiles of market wages. The Department of Labor (DOL) proposes to raise these thresholds significantly. Entry-level (Level I) wages could rise from the 17th percentile to the 34th percentile, aligning them with what is currently considered mid-level pay. The DOL estimates that the changes would increase the average certified wage by about $14,000 per year per position.Mitchell Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm, offers an important political qualification. “While Democrats may resist certain fees and restrictions on foreign students, Wexler believes that increased wage minimums for H-1B and employment-based green cards, as well as broader authority for employer enforcement, could find support among some congressional Democrats. “Those aren’t one-party issues as a rule,” he says.PERM: More scrutiny for employers and green card applicantsEmployment-based green card applicants could face another challenging period if the proposed changes to the PERM labour certification process move forward. The Department of Labour (DOL) is considering changes to recruitment requirements and additional protections for US workers, particularly in situations involving recent layoffs. The proposed overhaul had recently cleared White House review.There is also concern over the suspension of PERM processing involving eight major employers, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.The incoming Congress could demand explanations from the Department of Labor, according to the attorneys. Upadhyay says: “Congress can’t end the investigation. It can, however, demand the evidence behind it, question why only some companies were singled out, and probe the process. The most likely route to relief is a legal challenge by the companies themselves.”F-1 students: Is the US becoming a less attractive destination?For international students, particularly those from India, two policy changes are of concern: the proposed elimination of Duration of Status and the proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT). The Duration of Status rule was finalised but blocked by a federal court before it could take effect. It would replace the existing framework with fixed periods of admission, subject to extensions.DHS has proposed charging $70,000 for an initial OPT recommendation and $30,000 for subsequent periods, including STEM OPT extensions. Universities would be required to pay the fee before recommending a student for OPT and could potentially pass the expense on to students or employers.On this front, Khanna believes that the House Oversight Committee is where a Democratic majority can make itself felt fastest. Under House rules, the committee may investigate any matter at any time, even one assigned to another committee. It can compel testimony and the production of documents by subpoena. Officials involved in the $100,000 fee, the OPT fee and the EAD backlog could therefore be called to testify under oath, while the internal analyses behind these measures could be demanded.Immigration attorneys also believe litigation could be the quickest way to challenge the proposed OPT fee.H-4 spouses: Uncertainty over work authorisationThe automatic extension of Employment Authorisation Documents (EADs) has ended for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025. DHS subsequently issued a final rule making the change permanent.Khanna points out that Senate Democrats have already filed a resolution, S.J.Res. 99, against the interim version of this rule. However, the resolution would still require the President’s signature to take effect.The next concern is the possibility of eliminating the H-4 EAD programme altogether. Batra says: “Because the H-4 EAD has existed for more than a decade, DHS would be required to do more than simply change its mind. The agency would need to acknowledge its policy reversal, provide a reasoned basis for the change, and address the significant reliance interests of H-4 families and their employers. Given the program’s longevity and the economic impact of rescission, any attempt to eliminate H-4 work authorisation would likely face substantial legal and procedural hurdles.”What changes on January 3?The incoming Democratic Congress will have more opportunities to scrutinise the administration’s immigration actions. Hearings, investigations, subpoenas and funding negotiations could put pressure on federal agencies.But the attorneys do not expect the new congressional majority to automatically reverse the administration’s immigration agenda.Upadhyay believes that, for the immediate future, the courts and the presidential veto will matter more than the congressional majority.“Where House oversight can do the most good is on pretextual delays. This administration has been assassinating legal immigration by slowing it to a crawl, without changing a single rule. Since Dec 2025, when the State Department ordered an online-presence review of every H-1B and H-4 applicant, consulates in India have cut daily interviews and cancelled appointments wholesale. Individuals are now offered H-1B interview dates more than six months out, and H-4 spouses often find no appointment at all. At USCIS, a standalone H-4 EAD renewal is taking more than a year, and with automatic extensions gone, every month of delay past the card’s expiry is a month a lawfully present spouse cannot work. None of these nefarious, underhanded schemes, too numerous to count, appears in the Federal Register. The Oversight Committee can demand the staffing figures, the internal guidance and the emails behind these slowdowns, and put the officials responsible under oath. Like noxious black mould, furtive toxicity withers in daylight; dispelling secrecy is an important antidote,” Khanna emphasises.The incoming Congress may be able to subject immigration policy to greater scrutiny and use funding negotiations to press the administration. But with executive authority intact and major disputes continuing in the courts, the practical impact on H-1B workers, students, H-4 spouses and employment-based green card applicants will depend largely on how those legal and regulatory battles unfold.You use AI every day. articles.title: US midterm fallout: Trump's India envoy Sergio Gor may replace Marco Rubio - report
articles.summary: As Washington prepares to recover from the less than ideal performance of the Republican party during the midterms, reports suggest a possible overhaul in
articles.body: As Washington prepares to recover from the less than ideal performance of the Republican party during the midterms, reports suggest a possible overhaul in senior leadership.US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor has emerged as a possible contender for senior positions in president Donald Trump's administration following the recent setbacks in the midterm elections, with his name reportedly circulating for roles including White House chief of staff and secretary of state.Gor, a former senior White House aide and close Trump ally, has been discussed within the administration as a potential candidate for a bigger role during the second half of Trump's term, according to a report by The Washington Sun, citing 10 people familiar with internal discussions. There is also growing speculation among State Department officials that Gor is interested in a promotion.Well-connected within the administration and known for his direct access to Trump, Gor has increasingly taken part in high-level diplomatic engagements, acquiring influence beyond his role as ambassador to India. He is also seen as an important link between Washington and several Asian countries, as well as a close confidant of secretary of state Marco Rubio.According to the report, Gor's name has come up for several senior positions, including replacing Rubio as secretary of state or Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Some officials have also discussed the possibility of him taking over as deputy secretary of state from Chris Landau.Neither Rubio nor Wiles has indicated any intention of leaving their positions. However, speculation in Republican and State Department circles suggests Rubio could eventually leave the Cabinet to prepare for a potential presidential bid in 2028 or 2032. Wiles' position, meanwhile, is also believed to be under scrutiny within Trump's inner circle.Landau was also reportedly believed to be considering leaving after the midterms if Republicans lost control of Congress, anticipating potentially difficult congressional investigations. However, he subsequently denied having any plans to quit, telling The Sun that he had never indicated an intention to leave the State Department.Gor, however, dismissed the speculation, saying he had no interest in another position and had not discussed taking up a different role with anyone.Calling the report “complete and total b*******”, Gor praised Rubio as the most qualified and accomplished secretary of state, describing him as irreplaceable and a close friend. “I have zero interest in any other role,” he said.The State Department also rejected the claims. Assistant secretary for global public affairs Dylan Johnson said Rubio and Gor shared a strong professional relationship and personal friendship, dismissing the speculation as rumours based on anonymous sources. A White House official similarly described the report as fake, saying Gor had no interest in another position and believed Wiles and Rubio were doing a phenomenal job.Despite the denials, Gor's growing diplomatic profile has drawn attention within the administration. A Trump adviser told The Sun that the president “loves the guy”, crediting Gor with bringing deals to Trump during his years outside office rather than seeking favours from him.Since taking charge of the US embassy in New Delhi in November 2025, Gor has helped facilitate several high-level visits to India, including those by Rubio, commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and then-Army secretary Dan Driscoll. His responsibilities have also extended beyond India, with his dual role as ambassador and special envoy for South and Central Asia allowing him to participate in meetings with senior foreign officials, including Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.Rubio has visited India twice this year, and the two have travelled together frequently since Gor's appointment. They also appeared together in Atlanta at a G20 summit last week.Gor was also central to Rubio's visit to Uzbekistan last month, part of the Trump administration's efforts to deepen ties with resource-rich Central Asian countries. Born in Uzbekistan when it was part of the Soviet Union, Gor has used his background and regional connections in his additional role as special envoy for South and Central Asia.His approach to diplomacy is seen by some officials as closely aligned with Trump's emphasis on dealmaking and promoting American business interests.Gor, who worked on Trump's 2024 election campaign, has previously been linked to the business interests of the president's family. His publishing company has published Trump's books, and he is particularly close to Donald Trump Jr. Before leaving for India, Gor was sworn in as ambassador during an Oval Office ceremony at which Trump described him as a “great guy” and said he was “very proud” of him.His tenure in New Delhi has also attracted attention for his hands-on management style. According to two people familiar with the embassy's operations, Gor has exercised an unusual degree of control over personnel decisions, including pushing out career State Department employees and locally hired staff.Rubio had earlier defended Gor's appointment, telling The New York Times that his “access to the president” made him “an enormous asset” for both India and the State Department.However, whether Gor's connections would translate into a Senate-confirmed Cabinet position remains uncertain. All Senate Democrats voted against his confirmation as ambassador as part of a larger package of nominees.Before joining the Trump administration, Gor spent roughly a decade working on Capitol Hill, primarily for Republican senator Rand Paul. At the White House Office of Presidential Personnel, he was responsible for identifying and vetting candidates for thousands of political appointments across the federal government.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mid-air chaos: Multiple flights in Europe diverted due to bomb threats
articles.summary: Bomb threats have forced at least 12 passenger aircraft to divert or make precautionary landings across Europe on Thursday, triggering security checks at
articles.body: Bomb threats have forced at least 12 passenger aircraft to divert or make precautionary landings across Europe on Thursday, triggering security checks at airports in multiple countries for the second time in a week.An Aer Lingus flight, EI402, travelling from Dublin to Rome landed safely at Evreux airport in France, about 100 km west of Paris, after being diverted as a security precaution, the Irish airline said in a statement.A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted by Italian Air Force fighter jets before landing safely at Rome Fiumicino Airport. Italian police subsequently carried out security checks on the aircraft, but found no explosives, according to the airport authorities.In Belgium, a flight operated by Polish airline LOT landed at Brussels' Zaventem airport following a security alert. The airline later said that no dangerous or suspicious items had been found on board.Bulgaria also reported three aircraft making emergency landings following bomb threats. Two flights, originating from Copenhagen and Madrid, landed in Sofia, while a third aircraft travelling from London landed in Plovdiv, according to local media.In the Czech Republic, police said four aircraft heading to Prague had received threats involving the possible presence of improvised explosive devices. Authorities assessed the threats as low risk but said all necessary security measures had been activated and inspections would be carried out after landing.Separately, nearly 200 passengers were evacuated from a Wizz Air flight travelling from Milan to Bucharest after it received a bomb threat. The aircraft landed safely at Henri Coanda International Airport, where Romanian authorities initiated security procedures and deployed an explosives disposal team to inspect it.The latest incidents come two days after at least seven flights and a cruise ship received bomb threats, disrupting operations at airports across Europe. No explosive devices were found following Tuesday's alerts.Although no country has attributed responsibility for the threats, the incidents come amid growing concerns among European officials over what they describe as hybrid attacks and sabotage operations linked to Russia and Iran.This week, unidentified hackers also disrupted refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries and French blood banks, causing temperatures in fridges and freezers to rise.Some experts have suggested that hoax bomb threats could form part of a broader pattern of low-cost, difficult-to-trace disruption operations.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Iowa landlord lost $700,000 in what he described as a Ponzi scheme as his marriage fell apart; a court upheld a $351,446 divorce payment despite his claim that much of the property belonged to him before marriage
articles.summary: An Iowa landlord who said he lost roughly $700,000 in what he described as a Ponzi scheme has failed to overturn a $351,446 divorce payment to his former
articles.body: An Iowa landlord who said he lost roughly $700,000 in what he described as a Ponzi scheme has failed to overturn a $351,446 divorce payment to his former wife. The Iowa Court of Appeals upheld the award, rejecting his argument that much of the property at issue had been his before the marriage and should therefore have been excluded from the division, according to the court’s published decision on Justia U.S. Law.The case illustrates how courts treat premarital assets when they are mixed with marital property or affected by events during the marriage. The husband said a large part of the wealth belonged to him, but the appeals court said the trial court was within its discretion in ordering the payment.The dispute over propertyThe husband entered the marriage with substantial assets, including real estate and other investments. He argued that these holdings were premarital property and should not have been counted as part of the marital estate when the divorce was finalised. During the marriage, the value of some of those assets changed, and the husband later said that a large part of his wealth had been lost through a Ponzi scheme. He claimed the loss, estimated at around $700,000, should have reduced the amount he was required to pay his former wife, as per the report.The wife took a different view, arguing that the property had been commingled and that she was entitled to a fair share of the marital estate. The issue was whether the assets were still separate property, or had become marital property to be divided.The award of $351,446The trial court ordered the husband to pay $351,446 as a portion of the property settlement. He appealed, arguing that the amount was too high because much of the underlying property had been acquired before the marriage began.He also said the Ponzi scheme loss should have been given more weight because it lowered the value of assets available for distribution. The appeals court, however, found that the trial court had already considered these factors and had reached a reasonable outcome.The court said that the husband had not given sufficient evidence that the loss was not connected with the marriage or that it should have been treated as a separate reduction. Without clearer proof, the trial court’s decision stood.Why the court agreedIowa law gives courts wide discretion to divide property in a divorce based on what is fair under the circumstances. This includes looking at the length of the marriage, each spouse’s contributions and the source of the assets involved. The appeals court said the trial court did consider those factors. It also noted that the husband had not shown that the $351,446 payment was unjust or unsupported by the evidence. Thus, the court’s reasoning implies that even premarital assets may be considered part of the marital estate if they are commingled with marital funds or if their value increases during the marriage. This principle was key to the outcome of the case.What this means for landlordsThe case is a reminder for landlords and other property owners that premarital assets don't always stay separate in a divorce. If property is commingled, refinanced or otherwise affected during the marriage, it may be subject to division. This case is also illustrative of the value of keeping good records. If there is no record of what existed before marriage and how it changed over time, it may be difficult to establish that certain property should be excluded from the marital estate.For anyone facing a similar situation, the lesson is to be prepared with evidence. Courts will look at the full picture, including how assets were managed and whether they were treated as separate or marital property.A costly lessonThe husband’s claim that he lost $700,000 in a Ponzi scheme added another layer of complexity to the case. But the appeals court found that this did not change the basic fact that the trial court had made a fair division based on the evidence available.The $351,446 payment remains in place, and the husband’s attempt to reduce it has failed. For him, the result is an expensive lesson that divorce courts don’t just look at what’s on paper, but the whole history of the assets in question.It is a case that reminds anyone coming into a marriage with significant property of the importance of clear agreements and careful planning. Without them, even assets acquired before the marriage can become part of a larger dispute when the relationship ends.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US issues Forever stamp celebrating Diwali, features Rangoli created by Indian artist Sangita Bhutada
articles.summary: The United States Postal Service (USPS) has issued a new Forever stamp celebrating Diwali, featuring a colourful rangoli created by Indian artist Sangita
articles.body: The United States Postal Service (USPS) has issued a new Forever stamp celebrating Diwali, featuring a colourful rangoli created by Indian artist Sangita Bhutada. The release marks the second time the US postal service has dedicated a stamp to the festival of lights, with the first one issued in 2016.The US Embassy in India highlighted the new stamp in a post on X on Thursday, describing it as a Forever stamp celebrating Diwali. The stamp was officially unveiled on October 21 at the Embassy of India in Washington DC, in the presence of Indian Ambassador Vinay Mohan Kwatra and USPS senior vice-president Shibani Gambhir.The stamp features an eight-foot rangoli designed by Bhutada, a native of India who has been practising the traditional art form for nearly 30 years and is based in the Houston area. The artwork uses blue, orange, green, red and white colours against a purple background. It was created using coloured sand and starch-based powders and took eight to 10 days to complete.Photographer Bijay Dixit captured the original artwork, while Jennifer Arnold designed the stamp. William J Gicker served as its art director. The USPS has printed 20 million stamps, which are being sold in sheets of 20.The stamp is part of the Forever series, meaning it will remain valid for mailing a one-ounce first-class letter within the US even if postal rates increase in the future. Each stamp carries a value of 82 cents, with a sheet of 20 priced at $16.40.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'We are doing what the government won't': Greenpeace dumps nine giant boulders signed by celebrities including Benedict Cumberbatch and Simon Pegg into the North Sea to create a 45-square-mile underwater barrier against industrial fishing
articles.summary: The Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA), designated to safeguard marine wildlife, has recorded the highest level of bottom-trawling activity
articles.body: The Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA), designated to safeguard marine wildlife, has recorded the highest level of bottom-trawling activity among the UK's offshore protected sites. Now, in an unusual attempt to protect its marine biodiversity, Greenpeace activists have dropped nine giant limestone boulders onto the seabed, creating what the organisation describes as an underwater barrier against industrial fishing.The boulders, each weighing up to two tonnes, were deployed from Greenpeace's vessel Arctic Sunrise on October 31, approximately 50 km off England's eastern coast. The organisation announced the operation on November 2, claiming that the strategically placed rocks had effectively closed 116 sq km (approximately 45 square miles) of the protected area to bottom trawling.Why is Greenpeace targeting the North Sea?Bottom trawling involves fishing vessels dragging large, weighted nets across the seabed to catch fish. The method can damage sensitive underwater habitats, including corals, sponges and seagrass beds, while disturbing marine ecosystems and affecting species that depend on them. According to Greenpeace UK, bottom-towed fishing gear was used for at least 37,200 hours in the Southern North Sea protected area in 2025, more than at any other UK offshore MPA. Despite its protected designation, much of the site does not have restrictions on bottom trawling or dredging.The organisation argues that these activities threaten the food supply and habitats of harbour porpoises, small marine mammals that inhabit the region. The animals can also become accidentally entangled in fishing nets, potentially preventing them from reaching the surface to breathe. According to the Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), the Southern North Sea site is particularly important for harbour porpoises, supporting approximately 17.5% of the UK North Sea management-unit population.“With no restrictions on bottom trawling, the harbour porpoise – supposedly ‘protected’ in these waters – instead faces a barrage of daily threats. This includes the immediate threat of death by bycatch, noise pollution, weakened visibility, habitat destruction, and critically, the mass depletion of the prey these mammals rely on for feeding and survival,” Greenpeace said in a statement.Why activists took direct actionWill McCallum, Greenpeace UK's co-executive director, said the organisation had warned the government in June that it would take direct action if sufficient measures were not introduced to protect marine habitats. “Hulking great ships prowl our oceans day after day, stripping them of fish and killing precious wildlife like dolphins, sharks and sea birds. With our ship and a movement behind us, we're doing what the government isn't: Protecting our seas,” McCallum said.The campaigners argue that designating an area as a Marine Protected Area is not enough if destructive fishing activities are still permitted within its boundaries. Greenpeace has called on ministers to introduce stronger restrictions on bottom trawling across protected waters.The latest operation also has celebrity and political backing. Actors Simon Pegg and Benedict Cumberbatch, alongside several British public figures and MPs, signed the boulders before their deployment. The organisation said the signatures represented their support for stronger protection of marine ecosystems. Greenpeace also plans to patrol the area using the Arctic Sunrise in the coming days, aiming to discourage industrial fishing vessels from operating around the boulder placements.Did Greenpeace have permission to drop the boulders?The operation has raised questions about whether environmental activists can independently place objects on the seabed to prevent commercial fishing. Greenpeace has acknowledged that it did not obtain a marine licence before deploying the boulders, describing the move as a last resort after years of unsuccessful attempts to persuade the government to introduce stronger protections.Under Sections 65 and 66 of the UK's Marine and Coastal Access Act 2009, depositing a substance or object in the sea or on the seabed from a vessel is generally considered a licensable marine activity. Such activities require permission from the appropriate licensing authority unless a relevant exemption applies.The Marine Management Organisation (MMO), which oversees marine licensing in England, has not announced a specific enforcement outcome in its published notice about the latest deployment. However, the absence of a licence means the operation should not be described as officially authorised.Following the deployment, the MMO published the nine reported boulder positions on November 2, after Greenpeace relayed their coordinates to HM Coastguard. The regulator said the information was being shared to help fishing vessels and other sea users navigate the area safely. The MMO also clarified that it had not independently verified all the coordinates and advised mariners to take the reported positions into account when planning and conducting their activities.The UK government has also defended its broader marine protection framework. According to reporting by The Guardian, a government spokesperson said that legislation already protects marine sites, that damaging fishing activities have been banned in more than 100 locations and that further restrictions are being considered. The government also stressed that activities at sea must be conducted lawfully and safely.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A woman was left out of her aunt's £400,000 will after the pensioner branded her family 'The Rats'; a court rejected her inheritance challenge
articles.summary: A woman who was excluded from her great-aunt’s £400,000 estate has lost a legal challenge after a judge ruled that the pensioner had understood the
articles.body: A woman who was excluded from her great-aunt’s £400,000 estate has lost a legal challenge after a judge ruled that the pensioner had understood the decision to change her will. Doreen Stock, who died aged 86 in 2021, disinherited her great-nephew Ben Chiswick following a bitter family disagreement over a proposed care home stay. Stock reportedly referred to Chiswick’s parents as ‘The Rats’ after becoming upset by the suggestion. Despite claims that dementia had affected her judgment, the court found that she had retained the mental capacity required to make a valid will.Why was the £400,000 inheritance challenge rejectedAccording to The Independent, Ben Chiswick challenged his great-aunt’s will at Central London County Court, arguing that she had been suffering from dementia and was not capable of properly understanding the consequences of disinheriting him.Chiswick, a propulsion engineer living in the United States, said he had enjoyed a particularly happy relationship with Stock throughout his childhood. He described her as a fixture in his early life and questioned why she had suddenly decided to remove him from her inheritance.However, Judge Jane Evans-Gordon concluded that Stock had possessed the necessary mental capacity when she changed her will in 2020. Her decision followed evidence about the family disagreement, Stock’s relationship with her relatives and the circumstances surrounding the revised inheritance arrangements.The judge acknowledged that Stock had been unfair in her assessment of Chiswick’s parents, but stressed that being mistaken about another person’s behaviour did not automatically mean someone was incapable of making decisions.A care home suggestion triggered the family disputeThe disagreement began in 2019, when Stock’s niece Patricia Chiswick and her husband Brent were planning a three-week holiday in August.The couple had concerns about how Stock would manage during their absence and investigated the possibility of arranging a temporary stay at a residential care home. According to The Independent, they suggested that she spend the holiday period at a particular establishment and left a brochure for her.Stock initially agreed that a respite stay might be beneficial but later changed her mind. The suggestion left her deeply upset because she was fiercely independent and emotionally attached to her home.The judge found that the Chiswicks had not explicitly proposed that Stock move permanently into a care home. Instead, their immediate concern was whether she could manage during their holiday.Nevertheless, Patricia Chiswick admitted that there had been some hope that Stock would enjoy the experience sufficiently to consider moving into residential care permanently.That possibility may have contributed to Stock’s growing suspicion that her independence was under threat.Stock's attachment to her home shaped the decisionThe Independent reported that Stock had shared her south London property in Charminster Road, Mottingham, with her husband Samuel until his death in 2001.The pensioner had no children of her own and maintained a strong emotional connection to the house, which formed the principal part of her estate. The property was valued at approximately £400,000, making it the central asset in the inheritance dispute.Stock was described during proceedings as independent and occasionally stubborn, characteristics that helped explain why the prospect of residential care caused such distress.The disagreement was not limited to the care home suggestion. There had also been growing resentment over how the Chiswicks administered Stock’s lasting power of attorney.The court heard that Patricia had arranged a capacity assessment for her aunt. This further upset Stock, who apparently interpreted the assessment and care home discussions as signs that her family was attempting to undermine her independence.The Rats label reflected Stock's growing hostilityAs the relationship deteriorated, Stock became increasingly hostile towards Patricia and Brent Chiswick, eventually referring to them as The Rats.Judge Evans-Gordon said there was a concrete basis for Stock’s dissatisfaction with the couple, although she considered the pensioner’s judgment of their conduct unfair.The judge explained that Stock had been distressed to the point of tears by the care home suggestion and that her negative feelings towards the Chiswicks had intensified over time.According to The Independent, the judge accepted that the family’s actions had been well-intentioned, even if some of their decisions had been poorly judged. However, the emotional reaction did not establish that Stock lacked the ability to make decisions about her estate.A new will replaced the childhood inheritance arrangementStock’s original will, drawn up in 1986 when Ben Chiswick was a baby, had ultimately left her estate to him. But following the family breakdown, she began taking steps to revoke the lasting power of attorney and change her inheritance arrangements.In 2020, she replaced Chiswick as beneficiary, leaving her entire estate to her London-based nephew Simon Stock and his wife Catherine.The Independent reported that Simon had been particularly close to Doreen and was described by his barrister as the nearest thing to a son she had. Stock had also contributed towards his school fees when he was younger.The court heard that Simon and Catherine visited Doreen more frequently than the Chiswicks in her later years and helped her with everyday tasks. Ben, meanwhile, had not seen his great-aunt for several years before her death and had not spoken to her by telephone or written to her during that period.Judge upheld the pensioner's final wishesIn rejecting the inheritance challenge, Judge Evans-Gordon decided that Stock had retained the mental capacity to make a will between January and March 2020. She found that the pensioner’s resentment towards the Chiswicks, even if partly based on an unfair interpretation of their actions, did not make her decision irrational.The ruling means Simon and Catherine Stock inherit Doreen’s estate, including the Mottingham property, while Ben Chiswick receives nothing under the disputed will.You use AI every day. articles.title: Democrats got it right, but what next?
articles.summary: From January, Washington will have two competing centres of authority A Republican White House seeking to protect its programme and a Democratic Congress
articles.body: From January, Washington will have two competing centres of authorityA Republican White House seeking to protect its programme and a Democratic Congress elected to challenge it. How easily can Donald Trump secure laws, appointments and money?His appointments face a new gatekeeperThe Senate victory gives Democrats something House control alone could not: authority to reject nominees for federal judgeships, Cabinet posts and ambassadorships. Any Supreme Court vacancy would therefore become a major confrontation.His administration faces investigatorsDemocrats will control committees that can summon witnesses, seek documents and examine administration decisions. Hearings could force officials to defend their conduct publicly and reveal information the White House would prefer to withhold. Oversight becomes a continuing pressure.Money becomes a negotiationGovernment funding will require bargaining with the opposition. Democrats can seek concessions through spending legislation; Trump can refuse to sign it. That creates opportunities for compromise, alongside the danger of shutdowns and prolonged fiscal confrontations.But Trump has veto powerTrump can veto their bills. Overriding him requires two-thirds of members voting in each chamber. Under Senate rules, most legislation also needs 60 votes to overcome obstruction through a filibuster. Winning a majority therefore gives Democrats much greater power to block Trump than to enact their own programme.Nor does impeachment automatically mean removal. The House can bring charges, but conviction requires two-thirds of senators present.Trump retains substantial executive authority and can continue pursuing policies through presidential orders, subject to legal limits.The likely result is a presidency facing more resistance, scrutiny and bargaining. Each side will also have a new argument for 2028, that the other prevented it from delivering.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Thursday ruled out inviting Russian President Vladimir Putin to next year's G20 summit in the United Kingdom’s
articles.body: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Thursday ruled out inviting Russian President Vladimir Putin to next year's G20 summit in the United Kingdom’s Manchester.Asked by The Economist whether Putin would be invited to the meeting, Burnham replied: "No."The 2027 G20 summit is scheduled to take place in November in Manchester, a city in northwestern England where Burnham previously served as mayor.Burnham's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, Reuters reported.The development comes amid controversy over US invitation to Putin for this year's G20 meeting in Miami in December. In September, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said Washington had invited the Russian President, adding that the gathering would offer him an opportunity to engage with President Donald Trump and other world leaders, with possible discussions on Ukraine war peace plan.Moscow has said it “truly” appreciates the invitation but has not yet decided whether to accept it.Earlier, the US move drew criticism in Europe, where governments have been strengthening their militaries since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he feared the invitation would be viewed by Moscow as “encouragement to continue its aggressive policies”. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said it was “really very, very hard to understand this treatment” of Putin.Why Putin has stayed away from G20 summitsRussia continues to be a member of the G20 despite efforts by Western countries to isolate Moscow following its invasion of Ukraine. Leaders of countries hosting the annual summit traditionally invite all members of the grouping.However, Putin has not attended a G20 leaders' summit in person since the full-scale invasion. Russia has instead been represented at subsequent meetings by foreign minister Sergey Lavrov or other officials.His absence has often been linked to strained relations with Western countries, the possibility of confrontations with other leaders and an arrest warrant issued against him by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2023.The warrant accuses Putin of war crimes involving the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. It has restricted his ability to travel to countries that are parties to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC.Russia's continued membership of the G20 contrasts with its exclusion from the G8 format. In 2014, following Moscow's annexation of Crimea, the other seven members suspended their participation in the G8 and held their summit in Brussels without Russia, effectively reverting to the G7.You use AI every day. articles.title: US sanctions Chandigarh couple for aiding Iran's oil trade fraud - how did their network operate
articles.summary: The United States on Wednesday imposed fresh sanctions on several companies and individuals, including a Chandigarh-based businessman and his wife, for
articles.body: The United States on Wednesday imposed fresh sanctions on several companies and individuals, including a Chandigarh-based businessman and his wife, for allegedly helping Iran evade restrictions on its oil trade.According to a statement released by the US treasury department, Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, supported Iran's shadow fleet through a network involved in maritime fraud.The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's "Operation Economic Outcast", aimed at isolating Iran and cutting off its oil revenues, which Washington alleges are being used to fund its war with Israel and America.Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the US would take action against anyone supporting the Iranian regime."We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air," Bessent said."As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us," he added.What US allegesAccording to the treasury department, Sharma and Shahid allegedly defrauded maritime regulatory authorities in multiple jurisdictions to set up fake vessel flagging authorities and maritime classification societies.The Indian couple is accused of helping Iran's shadow fleet circumvent international restrictions by providing fraudulent vessel registration and certification services."Sharma and Shahid’s operations began as early as 2014, when the couple sought to impersonate the flagging authority of the Caribbean nation of Dominica," the treasury department said.It added that Sharma established Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. (Eswatini Maritime) in 2023. Despite being publicly disavowed by Eswatini authorities, the company allegedly continued to provide flagging services to vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including the sanctioned vessel PING SHUN (IMO 9231901).The department said the network also operated websites claiming to provide maritime services on behalf of countries that had not authorised them. These services included vessel flagging, seafarer training and certification, and vessel classification.It further alleged that several of these purported registries were not linked to registered companies, with the network using web domains to create websites that falsely claimed to represent the maritime authorities of different countries.Separately, the US also sanctioned Turkey-based Fugo Ground Services Inc for allegedly supporting Iran's heavily sanctioned aviation sector.According to the treasury department, the company provided ground handling and other services to several US-sanctioned Iranian airlines that continued to operate flights to Turkey. These included Iran Air Tour, Saha Airlines, Taban Airlines and Ata Airlines.The action is part of Washington's broader effort to choke off Iranian oil revenues and target networks accused of helping Tehran circumvent international sanctions.You use AI every day. articles.body: Elon Musk poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Republican campaign. Democrats countered with billionaire backers of their own and candidates who raised substantially more than their opponents. In the battle for Congress, both sides had money to spend. Republicans’ defeat showed what even an enormous financial effort could not guarantee.OpenSecrets’ pre-election tally put Musk’s contributions to federal political committees at $445 million, including $215 million to America PAC, the group he established, and $168 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, which backs Republican Senate candidates.Musk was the biggest donor, but the Republican funding network extended across technology, finance and other industries. A Brennan Center analysis, using disclosures through June, put venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz’s contributions to boost Republicans at $115 million. By mid-October, the 40 biggest donors had contributed $2.4 billion. Those supporting Republicans supplied more than three times as much as donors backing Democrats.Democrats had a different financial advantage. OpenSecrets projected Democratic congressional candidates would spend more than $2.2 billion, compared with approximately $1.4 billion for Republicans. Its October 30 tally of outside spending showed the reverse: conservative groups had spent over $2 billion, against $1.7 billion for liberal groups.Democrats also drew on substantial private fortunes. Soros-linked organisations Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform together contributed more than $102 million to liberal groups, while Michael Bloomberg’s contributions exceeded $100 million during the cycle.LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and his wife, Michelle Yee, contributed $41 million to Democratic-aligned groups.OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, contributed $25 million to Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. and another $25 million to Leading the Future, an AI-focused political group.Those were personal contributions. articles.title: Israel’s election deadlock: Bibi in a bind, but what changes for India, Iran and Gaza?
articles.summary: Fifty-three seats. A lead over every rival bloc. And perhaps no government to show for it.
articles.body: Fifty-three seats. A lead over every rival bloc. And perhaps no government to show for it. Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as the single-largest party in Israel’s new Knesset, and his bloc finished ahead of every rival camp.Yet inside President Isaac Herzog’s residence this week, the numbers appear to be shifting towards the man who came second.The numerical paradox at the heart of the election results has left Israel without a new government, Netanyahu without a majority and his challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, without an easy route to power.The final count gave Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset. Eisenkot’s Yashar-led opposition alliance won 48.The two Arab-led parties, the Joint List with 11 seats and Ra’am with eight, took a record 19. The magic number is 61. And nobody has it.Turnout hit 77.9 per cent, the highest since 1999, while Arab voter participation surged to approximately 77 per cent. Netanyahu, meanwhile, portrayed the surge in Arab voter turnout as an attempt to "hijack" the polls.Bibi in a bindIsraeli President Herzog received the certified results on Wednesday. The Central Elections Committee reviewed 9,069 polling stations and found no irregularities that compromised the vote.That undercut Netanyahu’s repeated and unsubstantiated claims that Arab parties had “stolen” the election with foreign help.The committee’s head, Justice Noam Sohlberg, warned that “election results, as lawfully determined, are binding on us all.” A separate Shin Bet inquiry into alleged foreign funding continues, though the attorney general has refused to let the agency question elected Arab officials without evidence.Herzog then broke with custom by meeting the smaller parties first and leaving Likud for last on Thursday evening.By Wednesday night, Eisenkot had secured the backing of parties holding 56 seats, putting him ahead of Netanyahu in the race for the mandate to form a government.United Torah Judaism, the ultra-Orthodox bloc that has long been Netanyahu’s ally, told Herzog it would back neither man. The Joint List had not yet said whether it would endorse Eisenkot or abstain.A lead in recommendations is not a government, and Herzog is not bound to follow the tally. He must choose whoever he thinks can actually build a coalition. The designated candidate then gets 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10 regardless. If nobody succeeds, Israelis could return to the polls early next year. Memories of political instability remain fresh, since the country held five elections between 2019 and 2022.Netanyahu's unfinished tasksAs Israel grapples with the political deadlock, the timing of the impasse is crucial, given the multiple agendas Netanyahu had on the table. The biggest of them is Iran.The war is paused, not finished. The US and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, a Pakistan-brokered ceasefire followed on April 8, and subsequent diplomatic efforts failed to produce a lasting settlement. The Strait of Hormuz remains a flashpoint, with American restrictions and military pressure continuing.Plans for a possible resumption of strikes were in place, with American and Israeli militaries drawing up detailed options, including a short and intense operation. Netanyahu even urged Trump to restart strikes immediately after the midterms, but Trump gave nothing away.Now, the prospect of renewed military action has been complicated by another development: Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in the midterms, with Democrats winning control of Congress. And Israel's war against Iran cannot be seen in isolation.US Vice President JD Vance, widely reported to have doubted the war from the outset, said it cost Republicans dearly. Trump, though, insisted he would “do it again”. However, the Democratic takeover of Congress, once the new lawmakers are sworn in, could complicate his ability to pursue another military operation, particularly given earlier attempts to curb his war powers.For Netanyahu, caretaker status could be a temptation, and a fresh operation might shift attention from coalition talks. But how far would Republicans be willing to go under Trump's leadership, especially after their midterm losses?The more reliable reading, therefore, is that Washington holds the decision. Israeli coalition arithmetic cannot force a resumption, but it may shape how eager Jerusalem is to ask for one.Meanwhile, Netanyahu's political rival Eisenkot's stance on Palestinian statehood is not fundamentally different.A former chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) from 2015 to 2019, Eisenkot has called the two-state formula a mistake, rejected Palestinian statehood and argued that Israel should retain overriding security control between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean.He wants Hamas stripped of its military power and removed from power in Gaza, and has pledged to replace its administration within 18 months through a US-backed arrangement or the use of force.He served in Netanyahu’s war cabinet before resigning in June 2024, but his complaint was primarily about execution, not aims.Eisenkot opposes Netanyahu’s far-right partners, criticises settler violence and questions some settlement plans, so the West Bank could see a more controlled approach. On Gaza itself, a change of prime minister would more likely change the method than the goal.What changes for 'chaver' IndiaFor India, the bilateral relationship looks sturdier than the politics.Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Israel in February, when the two sides announced more than a dozen agreements, discussed a free trade deal and agreed to admit 50,000 more Indian workers.Israeli analyst Alec Pollard told news agency PTI that the partnership goes beyond any one leadership. Yet a drawn-out government formation process could delay defence technology transfers expected by the end of this year.India’s larger exposure lies in the Gulf, with its trade with the Gulf Cooperation Council at about $178.63 billion in 2025-26 and roughly 10 million Indians living in the region.Iran matters through the Chabahar port, while the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor depends on regional stability.If strikes on Iran resume and Gulf infrastructure is hit, the impact on India would be felt through oil supplies and its diaspora long before it is felt through bilateral ties with Israel.New Delhi will therefore want stability, whoever finally governs in Jerusalem.In Tehran, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Ghalibaf said, “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” However, Trump's insistence that Iran must not be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons makes a thaw in relations unlikely in the near term.What's stopping Gadi's YasharEisenkot’s difficulty is that his bloc has sworn not to sit with Netanyahu, yet cannot reach 61 without Arab votes.Avigdor Liberman has been among the strongest opponents of relying on Arab parties, although his party has backed Eisenkot for the mandate.The Arab parties have offered something short of a partnership, with the Joint List’s Yousef Jabareen saying his party will not join an Eisenkot government but would vote with it in the Knesset, potentially enabling a minority government.Ra’am’s Mansour Abbas has said he would join if given the internal security portfolio. The opposition has set conditions for any such arrangement, including acceptance of Israel as a Jewish state, support for army conscription and a denunciation of Hamas.Dozens of protesters gathered outside Eisenkot’s home to oppose any Jewish-Arab alliance.The other route is no easier, as wooing the ultra-Orthodox parties would mean softening the opposition’s campaign pledge to end military service exemptions. Netanyahu, for his part, would need to peel away at least eight opposition lawmakers.Netanyahu has survived setbacks that once appeared decisive, and the numbers still leave room for another political comeback. But the ground has shifted this week.His key ally in Washington has lost control of Congress, his rivals are rallying behind Eisenkot, and the Arab vote he sought to delegitimise has emerged as a decisive factor in his political future.The coming weeks will determine whether Herzog's mandate leads to a new government or merely prolongs the political uncertainty.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Baseless allegation, why were you sharing tea?’: After 4-hour questioning, CJP leaders challenge Jitendra Singh to prove foreign funding claims
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) activist Saurav Das on Thursday hit back at Union minister Jitendra Singh over allegations of foreign funding
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) activist Saurav Das on Thursday hit back at Union minister Jitendra Singh over allegations of foreign funding behind the outfit's youth-led movement, demanding evidence and calling the claims baseless.His remarks came after Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde were questioned by the Delhi Police Crime Branch for around four hours in connection with two FIRs over the October 13 Jantar Mantar protest.Police sources said around 70 questions were put to the CJP leaders, some of which they did not answer.Das accused right-wing groups and extremist networks of running campaigns to malign the movement, alleging that the same narrative was now being repeated by a senior minister in the government."The allegation is baseless. The question of evidence is something we have been raising from day one, even before the first protest took place on June 6. Even before that, we had witnessed the kind of negative campaign being carried out against this movement and this youth-led agitation.""Our first press conference was held on June 3, and ever since then, we have been asking the same question: What is the basis of your so-called allegation? So far, no evidence or justification has been provided. It has been four to five months, and now the same lie that was being peddled by right-wing groups and extremist networks — whose only job seems to be to run paid campaigns to malign a very credible movement — is being repeated by a senior minister in the government. It is a shame..."Ashutosh Ranka questions Jitendra SinghRanka also challenged the minister over the foreign funding allegations, questioning why government representatives had held discussions with the CJP if the movement was allegedly backed by foreign entities."Ask Jitendra Singh—ask him: if there was foreign funding involved, why were they shaking hands with us? Why were they negotiating with us? Why were they sitting down and holding talks with us—sharing tea and breakfast? Ask him for an answer to that...Funding from Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, and America! You ignore all the real issues facing this country and keep falling back on the same tired, worn-out rhetoric ...You have no explanation for why votes are being stolen in this nation.""Why is this government shielding Gyanesh Kumar? You have no answer as to why exam papers are being leaked, or why there is such high unemployment in this country. Instead, you keep pushing that same 12-year-old, stale agenda—claiming that funding is coming from here or there. Ask Jitendra Singh about this. Why were they shaking hands with us? Why were they sitting with us, having tea and snacks ?"The CJP also posted a response on X, saying, "This is the shameful reality. A Union Minister can say anything and get away with it. This is precisely why even the Words of those occupying the highest chairs hold no Value today."CJP leaders questioned for 4 hours, asked around 70 questionsAccording to police, Das, Ranka and Shinde reached the Crime Branch office in Rajouri Garden around 11am on Thursday. Their questioning concluded around 3pm.Police sources said around 70 questions were put to them, but the leaders did not respond to some of them.The questioning was conducted by officers of the inspector rank, sources said.Speaking to reporters after leaving the Crime Branch office, Ranka described the questioning as a routine investigation into the October 13 incident and reiterated that the CJP leaders would cooperate with the authorities.The three leaders had earlier been summoned to join the investigation but did not appear on October 22. Ranka had then said they had informed the Crime Branch that they could not attend and were awaiting fresh dates. What are the Jantar Mantar protest FIRs against CJP leaders?The questioning relates to two FIRs registered at Connaught Place and Parliament Street police stations over the CJP's October 13 protest at Jantar Mantar. The cases were subsequently transferred to the Crime Branch for investigation.The police have alleged that CJP activists entered the denotified protest site through private premises and violated restrictions imposed at the location. The activists had staged a protest and unfurled the national flag at Jantar Mantar.Das and Ranka were detained following the protest and later released on the orders of the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court on October 21 after furnishing personal and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each.The SEM directed them to appear on every hearing date and comply with the conditions specified in their bonds and written undertakings.The two leaders also undertook not to breach peace or disturb public tranquillity, and not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is denotified in accordance with the law. They further agreed that any future demonstrations would be conducted within the constitutional framework.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Thursday compared Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav's statement about the upcoming Uttar Pradesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Thursday compared Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav's statement about the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly polls to a military commander staying away from the battlefield while his soldiers fight.Akhilesh Yadav, who served as Uttar Pradesh chief minister from 2012 to 2017, said on Tuesday that he would not contest the assembly elections, scheduled for early next year, and would instead become chief minister "directly from the Lok Sabha."Also Read | 'I become CM when I don't contest elections': SP chief Akhilesh Yadav rules out contesting UP assembly elections"I found this quite unusual. As a leader, you have to lead from the front. You have a responsibility to act like a commander who leads and guides soldiers on the battlefield, rather than sitting in a palace and watching them fight," Paswan told reporters in Varanasi.The Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) chief also questioned whether the SP president was apprehensive about an impending defeat."Akhilesh ji's statement that he will not contest the election but will take the oath is somewhat surprising. Is he afraid of defeat or concerned about his party's performance?" he asked.Paswan cited assembly elections held after the 2024 Lok Sabha polls; the BJP lost its parliamentary majority in the Lok Sabha polls but the saffron party-led coalition went on to win state elections in Maharashtra, where the Congress and its allies had secured more seats in the general elections."In the Lok Sabha elections, they (the opposition) secured votes by spreading lies and claiming that the Constitution and reservation were under threat. But now they appear worried that voters may not back them in the assembly elections, as happened in Maharashtra," added the LJP (RV) chief, whose party is an ally of the ruling BJP.The BJP won 33 of Uttar Pradesh's 80 Lok Sabha constituencies in 2024, down from 71 in 2014 and 62 in 2019. SP and Congress, who contested as allies, won 37 and six seats, respectively.Akhilesh Yadav's remark, also made in Varanasi, referred to the 2012 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, which the SP had won. Following the victory, his father and SP founder Mulayam Singh Yadav made him chief minister even though Akhilesh was then a Lok Sabha MP and had not contested the assembly elections.His successor, incumbent chief minister Yogi Adityanath, who will be seeking a third consecutive term, was also a Lok Sabha MP in 2017 and did not contest the assembly elections that year.Both leaders contested in 2022, after which Akhilesh Yadav became the leader of the opposition in the Uttar Pradesh assembly.
